h: Canals, coffee and a day in Worsley
p: The garden covers around 154 acres, so this is a place to pace yourself. Two to three hours lets you see the walled garden and a loop round the lakes, but keen gardeners can happily stay all day. Comfortable shoes are a must, and a waterproof is a good idea, because this is Greater Manchester after all.

The Paradise Garden is a favourite inside the walls, a calm, colourful space designed to make you slow down. Out in the wider grounds, Ellesmere Lake and the woodland paths give you room to breathe, and there's always something seasonal going on, from spring bulbs to autumn colour and winter structure. Talks, workshops and family events pop up through the year, so it's worth seeing what's on before you go.

Bridgewater is a living, growing garden, and it's fun to watch it mature. Come back in a few years and areas that were young planting will have filled out, so it's a garden that rewards repeat visits.

The garden's name comes from the Bridgewater Canal, which runs right alongside. It was built for the Duke of Bridgewater to carry coal from his mines at Worsley and opened in 1761, and it's often called the canal that kicked off Britain's canal age. Just down the towpath, Worsley village is a pretty spot with black-and-white buildings, the old Packet House and the Delph, where the canal tunnels once ran into the mines. Look out for the water, which turns a striking orange from the iron ore. Pubs and cafés in Worsley make it easy to round off the day with a bite to eat.
